title: Benefit measures: reliability, safety, environmental, financial

blocks.text: 7.4.1 Benefit Measures: Reliability, Safety, Environmental, Financial

GridCap's planning board meets to rank the tiny portfolio's eight projects. Finance brings a list sorted by NPV, and tiny's P004, a $3,000k breaker replacement, is on top. The distribution engineer objects: P003, a tower set replacement on the Coast, keeps 12,000 customers from losing power for four hours each time those towers fail, and NPV does not see a single one of them. The safety lead adds that vegetation work prevents fires. Each of them is right about something the others' numbers leave out.

Before any of this can go into a model, each of these claims has to become a number with a unit: a **benefit measure**. This lesson defines the four families of measures a utility's capital plan uses (reliability, safety, environmental and financial), computes them for every GridCap tiny project, and shows that each one ranks the projects in a different order. Lessons 7.4.2 to 7.4.4 then turn the four into one value per project.

GridCap is a fictional utility generated for this course. The consequence table, the customer count and the outage log in this lesson are invented too; no number here describes a real utility. Every project and asset ID in this lesson is the tiny portfolio's: tiny's P003 is a Coast tower set, while small's P003 (lesson 7.1.4) is a Valley circuit clearing, because each portfolio numbers its own projects from P001.
A Benefit Measure Counts One Consequence, in One Unit

A capital project is worth doing because of what it prevents or creates. Replacing a worn transformer prevents some of its future failures, and each failure would have had **consequences**: customers lose power, someone may be hurt, oil may burn, and the utility pays for an emergency repair. A **benefit measure** is one of those consequences, counted in one unit, as the amount the project changes it. The utility's job is to pick the measures, and each needs three things written down:

items: **What it counts.** "Customer-minutes of interruption avoided", not "reliability".
**Its unit.** Customer-minutes, incidents, tonnes, thousands of dollars.

**Its direction.** Every measure in this module counts something *avoided* or *gained*, so more is always better. A measure that counts something bad (minutes of outage *after* the project) has to be turned around before it can join the others; counting the *reduction* does that.

blocks.text: The four families of measures a utility's capital plan uses, with the measure this module picks for each:

rows: emissions avoided (fire, gas leaks, oil fires)

blocks.text: **CO2e** (carbon-dioxide equivalent) puts different greenhouse gases on one scale: a tonne of a gas counts as the tonnes of CO2 that would warm the climate as much. A breaker's insulating gas, SF6, warms it far more per tonne than CO2, so a leak of a few kilograms counts as tonnes of CO2e.
SAIFI Counts Interruptions and SAIDI Counts Minutes, per Customer Served

Reliability is the measure regulators watch most closely, and utilities report it with standard indices defined in IEEE Standard 1366. Two of them matter here. Let $`N_T`$ be the number of customers the utility serves, and let an outage log list, for each sustained interruption $`j`$, the customers it cut off, $`N_j`$, and the minutes until their power came back, $`r_j`$:

items: **SAIFI**, the System Average Interruption *Frequency* Index, counts **customer interruptions**: one customer losing power once is one customer interruption. Divided by the customers served, it is how many times the average customer lost power in the year.

**SAIDI**, the System Average Interruption *Duration* Index, counts **customer-minutes of interruption**: 1,000 customers out for 60 minutes are 60,000 customer-minutes. Divided by the customers served, it is how many minutes the average customer spent without power.
**CAIDI**, the Customer Average Interruption Duration Index, is the average restoration time of the customers who were interrupted.

blocks.text: Both indices count only **sustained** interruptions: under the IEEE method, those longer than five minutes. Shorter ones are **momentary** (a breaker that trips and recloses) and are tracked by a separate index. The denominator is all customers served, not the customers who were interrupted; dividing by those instead gives CAIDI's denominator, which is a different question.

Utilities also report each index with and without **major event days**, the storm days whose daily SAIDI is far above normal (the IEEE method sets the threshold from the previous five years). The two can differ a lot: the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported an average of about two hours a year without major events since 2013, and 5.8 hours in 2018 with them. A plan's benefit is normally stated against the "without major events" index, the part routine renewal changes.
Here is a year of GridCap outages (invented), eight of them, two momentary:

def reliability_indices(outages: list[Outage], customers_served: int) -> dict[str, float]:
    """SAIFI, SAIDI and CAIDI of a year's outage log; momentary outages do not count."""
    sustained = [o for o in outages if o.minutes > SUSTAINED_MINUTES]
    interruptions = sum(o.customers for o in sustained)
    customer_minutes = sum(o.customers * o.minutes for o in sustained)
    saifi = interruptions / customers_served
    saidi = customer_minutes / customers_served
    return {"SAIFI": saifi, "SAIDI": saidi, "CAIDI": saidi / saifi if saifi else 0.0}

log = [Outage(12_000, 240), Outage(4_000, 300), Outage(9_000, 3), Outage(1_500, 180),
       Outage(400, 360), Outage(6_000, 90), Outage(20_000, 2), Outage(1_200, 150)]
indices = reliability_indices(log, CUSTOMERS_SERVED)

customers served 600,000; 8 outages, 2 of them momentary
SAIFI 0.0418 interruptions per customer
SAIDI 8.69 minutes per customer
CAIDI 207.7 minutes per interrupted customer

Check it by hand. The six sustained outages interrupted 12,000 + 4,000 + 1,500 + 400 + 6,000 + 1,200 = 25,100 customers, so SAIFI is 25,100 / 600,000 = 0.0418. Their customer-minutes add up to 5,214,000, so SAIDI is 5,214,000 / 600,000 = 8.69 minutes. The 20,000 customers of the 2-minute outage count in neither index: a momentary outage is not a sustained interruption, however many customers it touches.

A project changes these indices by removing customer interruptions and customer-minutes from future years. Because the denominator $`N_T`$ is the same for every project, a project's **cut in SAIDI** is just its customer-minutes avoided divided by $`N_T`$, and its cut in SAIFI is its customer interruptions avoided divided by $`N_T`$. The two carry the same information as the counts, in a different unit; lesson 7.4.2 shows why that difference in unit must not change any decision.
<!-- practice 1 -->
Expected Failures Avoided Turn Into Every Non-Financial Measure

Where does a project's "customer-minutes avoided" come from? From the failures it prevents. Lesson 6.6.4 (and lessons 7.3.1 to 7.3.4, *Asset risk*) model each GridCap asset's failures with a Weibull curve of shape $`\beta`$ and scale $`\eta`$ years. If a failed asset is repaired just enough to run again, the expected number of failures between ages $`a`$ and $`a + h`$ is
N(a, h) = \Big(\frac{a + h}{\eta}\Big)^{\beta} - \Big(\frac{a}{\eta}\Big)^{\beta}

An intervention makes the asset younger. As in lesson 6.6.4, give each intervention a **depth** $`d`$: the asset's age becomes $`(1 - d)\,a`$. This module uses $`d = 1`$ for a replacement, rebuild or undergrounding (the asset is new), $`0.8`$ for clearing or widening a vegetation corridor, and $`0.5`$ for a repair or a trim (lesson 7.3.4 writes the same reset the other way round, as the share of its age the asset keeps; the section *Two Renewal Conventions, One Failure Model* below compares the two). Benefits are counted over an **evaluation window** of 10 years from the plan's first year, 2027 to 2036. A project started in year $`t`$, on an asset of age $`a_t`$ by then, has $`h_t = 2027 + 10 - t`$ years of the window left and avoids
F_{i,t} = N(a_t,\, h_t) - N\big((1 - d_i)\,a_t,\; h_t\big)
expected failures: those the old asset would have had, less those the renewed one will have.

def failures_avoided(portfolio: Portfolio, project: Project, start: int) -> float:
    """Expected failures the project avoids from its start to the end of the evaluation window."""
    asset = portfolio.asset(project.asset_id)
    first = portfolio.years[0]
    age = asset.age + (start - first)                  # the asset ages while it waits
    years = first + EVALUATION_YEARS - start            # benefit years left in the window
    after = (1 - DEPTH[project.intervention]) * age
    return (failures(age, asset.weibull_beta, asset.weibull_eta, years)
            - failures(after, asset.weibull_beta, asset.weibull_eta, years))

Every non-financial measure is then failures avoided times **what one failure does**, in that measure's unit. That per-failure consequence depends on the kind of asset: a tower set carries a transmission line that feeds many customers, a pole only a street. GridCap's table, invented for this module:

"Safety incidents per failure" is a probability-weighted count: 0.08 means that, on average, one tower failure in 12.5 hurts someone or creates a public hazard (a fallen conductor, a fire). So for project $`i`$ on an asset of kind $`k(i)`$, with customers $`C_k`$, restoration minutes $`M_k`$, incidents $`S_k`$ and emissions $`E_k`$ per failure:
For tiny's P003, the tower set from the opening, started in its only year, 2027:

P003 Coast tower set replace (A003): 0.574 expected failures avoided
  each cuts off 12,000 customers for 240 minutes
  customer interruptions avoided  6,888  -> SAIFI cut 0.0115
  customer-minutes avoided  1,653,216  -> SAIDI cut 2.76

0.574 failures avoided times 12,000 customers is 6,888 customer interruptions; times 240 minutes more, 1,653,216 customer-minutes. Spread over GridCap's 600,000 customers, that is 2.76 minutes of SAIDI, summed over the ten years of the window. These are **expected** values: P003 will not prevent 0.574 of a failure. Either the towers would have failed or not; 0.574 is the average over many possible futures, which is what a plan that treats many assets should count.

The same structure, probability of failure times consequence, is the risk of lessons 7.3.1 to 7.3.4 (*Asset risk*, lesson 7.3.3), there in dollars. Here the consequence is stated in each measure's own unit.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Two Renewal Conventions, One Failure Model
Lesson 7.3.4 also values a renewal by the failures it removes from the asset's Weibull curve, but it writes the renewal down differently. Side by side:

rows: $`\rho`$, the share of its age the asset **keeps**
$`d`$, the depth: the share of its age **taken away**
$`\rho`$ times the age it had reached
$`(1 - d)`$ times its age in the start year
the year after the work ends; it ages during the work
at the start of the start year
CoF times failures avoided, discounted at 7%
failures avoided times each measure's consequence, undiscounted

blocks.text: The two parameters are one number seen from opposite ends: $`d = 1 - \rho`$. A repair keeps half its age ($`\rho = 0.5`$) and has half taken away ($`d = 0.5`$); a replacement keeps none ($`\rho = 0`$, $`d = 1`$). (Lesson 7.2.4 uses $`\rho_i`$ for something unrelated, GridCap's benefit ratio.)

Only clearing and widening disagree. Lesson 1.1.2 gave every partial intervention the same 0.5, and lessons 7.3.1 to 7.3.4 kept it. This module gives corridor clearing and widening a deeper reset, $`d = 0.8`$ (that is, $`\rho = 0.2`$): taking a corridor back to its full cleared width removes most of the growth that causes its outages, where a trim cuts back only what is nearest the line. Both values are assumptions about the fictional GridCap, not measurements; a utility sets them from its own records of how failure rates change after each kind of work.
To see what each difference does, the program below counts expected failures avoided (not dollars) on 7.3.4's year-by-year age path and compares them with this lesson's formula:

def failures_by_age_path(asset, window, start: int, duration: int, keep: float) -> float:
    """Expected failures avoided over the window, year by year, on lesson 7.3.4's age path."""
    first, done = window[0], start + duration
    total = 0.0
    for y in window:
        before = asset.age + (y - first)
        after = before if y < done else keep * (asset.age + (done - first)) + (y - done)
        total += (failures(before, asset.weibull_beta, asset.weibull_eta, 1)
                  - failures(after, asset.weibull_beta, asset.weibull_eta, 1))
    return total
Read the columns left to right, one difference at a time.

items: **No time for the work, keep $`1 - d`$:** the age path gives exactly this lesson's numbers, in every row. The yearly expected counts add up to $`N(a, h)`$ over the window, so this lesson's formula is 7.3.4's method with zero years of work.

**The work takes its years:** the benefit falls for every project but P005, because the old asset keeps failing until the crew is done. Tiny's P006, two years of work, drops from 1.082 to 0.872, about a fifth. (P005's columns happen to agree to three decimals.)
**7.3.4's $`\rho`$:** only P008, the widening, changes, from 0.088 to 0.050.

blocks.text: So there is one method, and this lesson uses a short form of it. **To value a renewal, follow the asset's age year by year with and without the work** (lesson 7.3.4): it ages through the years of work, then keeps the share $`\rho`$ of the age it had reached and ages again; each year's benefit is the drop in expected failures times what one failure does, discounted if it is money. This lesson's $`N(a_t, h_t) - N((1 - d)\,a_t, h_t)`$ is that method with the years of work left out and nothing discounted, written with $`d = 1 - \rho`$. It keeps each measure one difference a reader can check by hand, and it counts customer-minutes, incidents and tonnes in their own units, which this module does not discount: a customer-minute in 2036 counts as much as one in 2028.

The rest of the course keeps both, each for its own job. The risk objective that section 8 trades against NPV is 7.3.4's, age path, time for the work and lesson 1.1.2's $`\rho`$ included, because it is stated in dollars beside NPV. The value function of lessons 7.4.2 to 7.4.4 is built on this lesson's measures and depths. A utility that wants its value function on the full method changes `failures_avoided` to sum along the age path, and every coefficient after it follows.
Financial Benefit Is NPV, and Each Consequence Is Counted Once

The financial measure is the project's **net present value** at its start year, $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$ in $k: its money benefits discounted to today, less its discounted cost. Lessons 7.2.1 to 7.2.4 (*Financial evaluation*) teach how it is computed; GridCap stores it as `Project.npv[start]`.

A failure also has a money consequence: the emergency repair. GridCap records it as the asset's `cof` in $k, and lesson 7.3.4 turns it into a risk reduction in dollars. Is it inside GridCap's NPV? No. Lesson 7.2.4 rebuilt every NPV entry from three things: the project's cost profile, a benefit equal to its capex times a **benefit ratio** drawn between 1.15 and 2.05, and a **decay** of 3% to 8% of that benefit per year of delay. No term uses `cof` or the failure curve. GridCap's NPV is a stand-in for the money case finance would bring, and it does not say what that money is.

So the course counts the avoided repair cost in exactly one place: the risk objective of lesson 7.3.4, which section 8 puts beside NPV as a second objective and trades against it at a stated price. Counted there, it must not come back in the value function too, so the value function does **not** add $`F \times \text{cof}`$ as a fifth measure. Adding it would count the same dollars twice, and a doubly counted effect gets twice the weight it deserves in the final decision. The rule is about where the dollars already sit. With a real utility's NPV built from avoided repair bills, the repair cost is inside NPV, and it is added neither as a fifth measure nor as a separate risk objective summed with that NPV; GridCap's NPV has no such term, which is why section 8 may weigh GridCap's NPV and risk against each other without counting anything twice. The UK government's multi-criteria analysis manual makes the same rule for public appraisals: the same impact may be *shown* from several points of view, but it is counted once when options are compared.

The practical test from that manual: take two projects that are identical in every measure except one, say customer-minutes. Would the board prefer the one with more? If yes, customer-minutes carry value that NPV does not, and they belong in the value function. If the board says "no, the customer-minutes are already priced in the NPV", then they are a double count and must go. Reliability, safety and environment pass that test at GridCap: none of them is in its NPV.

Correlated is not the same as doubly counted. Tiny's P006 scores high on reliability, safety and emissions because all three come from the same failures avoided. That is fine: each counts a different consequence of those failures (customers in the dark, people hurt, gas released), and the board values each separately.
Each Measure Ranks the Projects Differently
Here are all eight tiny projects, each started as early as it can, in all four measures (SAIDI is the customer-minutes column divided by 600,000):

P003    tower        replace       0.574  1,653,216   2.76      0.046   0.57     576
P004    breaker      replace       0.312    168,387   0.28      0.009   2.49   2,120
P005    circuit      trim          0.095     17,092   0.03      0.014   2.37     123
P006    transformer  replace       1.082  1,298,153   2.16      0.065  16.23   1,247
P007    transformer  repair        0.957  1,148,809   1.91      0.057  14.36     265

best by reliability   (customer-minutes): P003 P006 P007 P001 P002 P004 P008 P005

Four measures, three different winners. P004 tops the finance list and is last on safety. P003 tops reliability and is next to last on emissions. P007, a $290k repair, is second on safety and emissions and sixth on NPV. Any one list would hand the board a plan that ignores what the other three people at the table care about.

So the board needs **one** number per project that weighs all four, and a model needs it too: a MILP has one objective. Combining measures in different units is not a matter of adding them, and lesson 7.4.2 shows what goes wrong when you try.
Summary

items: **A benefit measure counts one consequence, in one unit.** Write down what it counts, its unit, and its direction; count reductions so that more is always better.

**SAIFI counts interruptions and SAIDI counts minutes, per customer served.** SAIFI = customer interruptions / customers served; SAIDI = customer-minutes / customers served; only sustained (over five minutes) interruptions count. GridCap's log gives SAIFI 0.0418 and SAIDI 8.69.

**Expected failures avoided turn into every non-financial measure.** Failures avoided (from the Weibull curve and the intervention's depth) times what one failure does: P003 avoids 0.574 failures, 1,653,216 customer-minutes.

**Two renewal conventions share one failure model.** This lesson's depth is lesson 7.3.4's share kept turned around, $`d = 1 - \rho`$, and its formula is 7.3.4's year-by-year age path with no years of work and no discounting. Clearing and widening take $`d = 0.8`$ here and $`\rho = 0.5`$ there; section 8's risk objective uses 7.3.4's, this module's value function this lesson's.

**Financial benefit is NPV, and each consequence is counted once.** GridCap's NPV has no repair-cost term; the avoided repair cost is counted once, in lesson 7.3.4's risk objective, so it is not added to the value function as well.
**Each measure ranks the projects differently.** On GridCap tiny, reliability, safety and finance each pick a different first project.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** U.S. Energy Information Administration, [Electric Power Annual, Table 11.1, Reliability Metrics of U.S. Distribution System](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_11_01.html) (what SAIDI and SAIFI count, and the IEEE major-event-day rule); EIA, [U.S. customers experienced an average of nearly six hours of power interruptions in 2018](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=43915) (SAIDI with and without major events); T&D World, [Understanding Distribution Reliability Metrics](https://tdworld.com/overhead-distribution/article/21157348/understanding-distribution-reliability-metrics) (SAIFI, SAIDI, CAIDI and MAIFI in plain words); UK Department for Communities and Local Government, [Multi-criteria analysis: a manual](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/7612/1132618.pdf) (2009), section 5.4.4.5 on double counting.
Challenges

items: A storm interrupts 50,000 customers for 20 hours on one day. Compute what it adds to GridCap's SAIDI, then say whether a renewal plan should be judged on that day.
Two outages each interrupt the same 1,000 customers for 60 minutes. What do they add to SAIFI? Is that "1,000 customers interrupted" or "2,000 customer interruptions"?

P007 (repair) avoids 0.957 failures and P006 (replace) avoids 1.082, on the same transformer. Why so close, when one makes the asset new and the other only halves its age? Look at the asset's age and its $`\beta`$.

blocks.text: Design Note: Measures Before Weights

It is tempting to start with the weights ("safety matters most") and fill in measures later. The order matters the other way round. A weight means nothing until you know what one unit of its measure is (lesson 7.4.3), and the arguments that slow a value function down for months are nearly always about what a measure counts: does vegetation work prevent fires or only outages, are customer-minutes counted with or without major events, is the repair bill in NPV or not. Settle the measures, their units and their sources first, and write them down in a table like the one above.
